To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

online social media support and enhance friendship in ways that reflect the key dimensions of Aristotelian virtue friendship, particularly reciprocity, empathy and the shared life, and that these developments are consistent with a contemporary Aristotelian theory that conceives of the good life in terms of the complete friendships of virtue.
the four dimensions of ‘virtues friendships’ are supported by online social media and that this support may be sufficient in the contemporary world.

(1) the Aristotelian ideal of ‘complete’ friendships is still relevant to our understanding of human flourishing, but (2) online friendships are not ‘complete’ friendships in the Aristotelian sense because they do not involve shared activities in a shared space, and (3) this is problematic, but (4) it is not clear that the Aristotelian conception of the shared life is the only way in which human beings can flourish, or even the best way.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ethical implications of new social media for friendship.
the ethical significance of friendship, and in particular, the ethical significance of the new social media.
the ethical implications of the growing use of social networking sites such Facebook and Twitter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
online social media can support the flourishing of virtue friendship in some ways, but not in others.
new social media are not the ideal medium for the flourishing of virtue friendship.
new social media, while supporting and strengthening friendship, are not yet able to provide complete friendships.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social media is a good tool to help you connect and interact with others.

we have found that the use of new media, especially social media, can be used to strengthen and enrich our relationships with our friends, and can be a useful tool for maintaining and building friendships, but that it cannot be used as a substitute for face to face relationships.
the use of social media can support friendship, but it is not a substitute for face-to face communication and interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while online social media may be useful tools for the cultivation of ‘virtue friendships,’ the cultivation of these friendships remains a deeply personal, face-to-face, and often local process.
the widespread and growing use social networking sites like Facebook and Twitter is not only ethically significant, but also raises a host of important questions for applied ethical research.
the widespread and growing use social media for socializing and networking has the potential to strengthen existing friendships, and to foster new ones.
